Adult Electric catfish reach a maximum recorded total length of 122 cm [Li = 122 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the family Malapteruridae. Field surveys and museum records consistently indicate that individuals rarely exceed this value, with growth trajectories decelerating markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity. The onset of reproductive capability occurs at a relatively modest size of 17.4 cm [Lp = 17.4 cm] total length, a threshold that is reached within the first year of life under optimal thermal conditions. This early maturation is energetically costly but appears to be an adaptive response to high predation pressure on juvenile cohorts. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the substantial gap between length at puberty and ultimate length reflects a prolonged adult growth phase, during which individuals invest heavily in somatic tissue accumulation while maintaining reproductive output. The robust body plan of this species, combined with its powerful electric organ discharge used for both predation and defense, allows large adults to dominate benthic habitats in the slow-moving river systems of tropical Africa.

Eggs of the Electric catfish are relatively large, with a diameter of approximately 7 mm, and the resulting wet weight at birth is calculated to be 0.18 grams [Wwb = 0.18 grams] based on the spherical volume of the egg. This substantial yolk reserve supports an extended endotrophic larval phase during which the yolk-sac larva remains entirely dependent on endogenous nutrients. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], eclosion occurs after an incubation period of 11 days [ab = 11 days], a duration consistent with the relatively large egg size and slow developmental rate characteristic of siluriform fishes. Following hatching, the yolk-dependent larva continues to absorb its yolk reserves for several more days before initiating exogenous feeding. The significant investment in egg volume suggests a strategy favoring offspring quality over quantity, a pattern often observed in species occupying stable, resource-limited environments. Comparisons with related taxa indicate that this egg diameter is among the largest recorded within the Malapteruridae.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Electric catfish can reach 20,000 grams [Wwi = 20,000 grams], reflecting a considerable capacity for somatic growth over the lifespan. This mass, equivalent to approximately 20 kilograms, is among the highest documented for electric catfishes and is associated with a piscivorous diet that becomes increasingly dominant as individuals grow. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty is only 52.7 grams [Wwp = 52.7 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. The dramatic difference between the weight at maturity and the ultimate weight underscores a life-history strategy in which a prolonged period of post-pubertal growth precedes the attainment of maximum body size. Large adults enjoy reduced vulnerability to predators and likely achieve higher reproductive success through increased fecundity and competitive dominance. Field studies have shown that individuals exceeding 10,000 grams are almost exclusively reproductively active adults that occupy the deepest pools within their riverine habitats.

Maximum lifespan in the Electric catfish has been estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when animals are maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] under captive conditions. This longevity, recorded in aquaria and research facilities, is consistent with a relatively slow life-history pace characterized by delayed senescence and sustained reproductive activity well into later life stages. The same thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] that supports maximal lifespan also influences the rate of embryonic development and early growth, as discussed above. Natural mortality in the wild is likely higher due to predation, disease, and environmental stochasticity, but the species' robust physiology and defensive electric organ undoubtedly contribute to its ability to reach advanced ages. Comparative analyses within Siluriformes suggest that a lifespan of 7 years is moderate, falling between short-lived tropical species and the decades-long lifespans observed in some large catfishes. Senescence in captive specimens typically manifests as a gradual decline in feeding activity and responsiveness before eventual physiological death.

Females of this species produce relatively small clutches for a large-bodied siluriform. Gravid individuals extrude between 200 and 400 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 200 and 400 eggs per spawning event], a fecundity that is modest given the considerable ultimate body mass. Spawning occurs approximately once per year [F_R_i = Spawning occurs approximately once per year], typically during the rainy season when elevated water levels flood marginal vegetation and create optimal nursery habitat for the yolk-sac larvae. The combination of low clutch size and annual spawning frequency results in a limited annual reproductive output, a pattern consistent with the substantial per-offspring investment reflected in the large egg diameter and a 0.18 gram [Wwb = 0.18 gram] birth weight. This life-history configuration aligns with that of an equilibrium strategist, prioritizing offspring survival in a stable environment over numerical productivity.
